# FDG8014

> DO NOT use `ArrayList` or `List<T>` in public APIs.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 8.3 Collections.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG8014, CA1002
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application none, test none
- Status: draft

Message: Do not use ArrayList in the signature of '{0}'

Library only: the text scopes it to public APIs. CA1002 reports List<T> as the type of a parameter, return value, property or field of an externally visible member (probe with SDK 10.0.402; an override was not reported). FDG8014 reports System.Collections.ArrayList in the same places: the type of a parameter, a return value or the result of a returned Task<T> or ValueTask<T>, a property or indexer, or a field of an externally visible member. Overrides and interface implementations are not reported, since their signature comes from another member. Types that only use ArrayList or List<T> as a type argument (IEnumerable<List<T>>) are not seen, so coverage is partial. Changing the type changes the public signature, so the fix is breaking; there is no code fix.

## From the book

These types are data structures designed to be used in internal implementation, not in public APIs. `List<T>` is optimized for performance and power at the cost of cleanness of the APIs and flexibility. For example, if you return `List<T>`, you will never be able to receive notifications when client code modifies the collection. Also, `List<T>` exposes many members, such as `BinarySearch`, that are not useful or applicable in many scenarios. Sections 8.3.1 and 8.3.2 describe types (abstractions) designed specifically for use in public APIs.

Instead of using these concrete types, consider `Collection<T>`, `IEnumerable<T>`, `IList<T>`, `IReadOnlyList<T>`, or other collection abstractions.

```csharp
// bad design
public class Order {
  public List<OrderItem> Items { get { ... } }
  ...
}
// good design
public class Order {
  public Collection<OrderItem> Items { get { ... } }
  ...
}
// also good design
public class Order {
  public IList<OrderItem> Items { get { ... } }
  ...
}
```
